{{Short description|Concept in cryptography}}
In [[cryptography]], a '''hybrid cryptosystem''' is one which combines the convenience of a [[public-key cryptosystem]] with the efficiency of a [[Symmetric-key cryptography|symmetric-key cryptosystem]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Shoukat |first=Ijaz Ali |date=2013 |title=A Generic Hybrid Encryption System (HES) |journal=Research Journal of Applied Sciences, Engineering and Technology |url=https://maxwellsci.com/jp/mspabstract.php?jid=RJASET&doi=rjaset.5.4793 |access-date= |volume=5 |issue=9 |pages=2692–2700 |doi=10.19026/rjaset.5.4793 |language=en|doi-access=free }}</ref> Public-key cryptosystems are convenient in that they do not require the sender and receiver to share a [[Shared secret|common secret]] in order to communicate securely.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Paar|first1=Christof|url=https://www.crypto-textbook.com/download/Understanding-Cryptography-Chapter6.pdf|title=Understanding Cryptography: A Textbook for Students and Practitioners|last2=Pelzl|first2=Jan|last3=Preneel|first3=Bart|publisher=Springer|year=2010|isbn=978-3-642-04100-6|chapter=Chapter 6: Introduction to Public-Key Cryptography}}</ref> However, they often rely on complicated mathematical computations and are thus generally much more inefficient than comparable symmetric-key cryptosystems. In many applications, the high cost of encrypting long messages in a public-key cryptosystem can be prohibitive. This is addressed by hybrid systems by using a combination of both.<ref name=":3">{{Cite book|last1=Deng|first1=Juan|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/computer-science/hybrid-encryption|title=Handbook on Securing Cyber-Physical Critical Infrastructure|last2=Brooks|first2=Richard|publisher=Elsevier|year=2012|isbn=978-0-12-415815-3|pages=655–676|chapter=Chapter 26 - Cyber-Physical Security of Automotive Information Technology}}</ref>

A hybrid cryptosystem can be constructed using any two separate cryptosystems:
* a [[key encapsulation mechanism]], which is a public-key cryptosystem
* a [[Symmetric-key algorithm|data encapsulation scheme]], which is a symmetric-key cryptosystem

The hybrid cryptosystem is itself a public-key system, whose public and private keys are the same as in the key encapsulation scheme.<ref name="cramer-shoup" />

Note that for very long messages the bulk of the work in encryption/decryption is done by the more efficient symmetric-key scheme, while the inefficient public-key scheme is used only to encrypt/decrypt a short key value.<ref name=":3" />

== Implementations and standards ==
All practical implementations of public key cryptography today employ a hybrid system. Examples include the [[Transport Layer Security|TLS]] protocol <ref>{{Cite web|last=Fox|first=Pamela|title=Transport Layer Security (TLS) (article)|url=https://www.khanacademy.org/computing/computers-and-internet/xcae6f4a7ff015e7d:online-data-security/xcae6f4a7ff015e7d:secure-internet-protocols/a/transport-layer-security-protocol-tls|access-date=2022-02-06|website=Khan Academy|language=en}}</ref> and the [[Secure Shell|SSH]] protocol,<ref>{{Cite web|last=Ellingwood|first=Justin|title=Understanding the SSH Encryption and Connection Process {{!}} DigitalOcean|url=https://www.digitalocean.com/community/tutorials/understanding-the-ssh-encryption-and-connection-process|access-date=2022-02-06|website=www.digitalocean.com|language=en}}</ref> that use a public-key mechanism for key exchange (such as [[Diffie–Hellman key exchange|Diffie-Hellman]]) and a symmetric-key mechanism for data encapsulation (such as [[Advanced Encryption Standard|AES]]). The [[OpenPGP]]<ref>{{Cite web|title=RFC 9580 - OpenPGP|url=https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9580|access-date=2024-08-02|website=datatracker.ietf.org|date=July 2024 |last1=Wouters |first1=Paul |last2=Huigens |first2=Daniel |last3=Winter |first3=Justus |last4=Yutaka |first4=Niibe }}</ref> [[file format]] and the [[PKCS#7]]<ref>{{Cite web|title=RFC 2315 - PKCS #7: Cryptographic Message Syntax Version 1.5|url=https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2315|access-date=2022-02-06|website=datatracker.ietf.org|date=March 1998 |last1=Kaliski |first1=Burt }}</ref> file format are other examples.

Hybrid Public Key Encryption (HPKE, published as [https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9180/ RFC 9180]) is a modern standard for generic hybrid encryption. HPKE is used within multiple IETF protocols, including [[Messaging Layer Security|Messaging Layer Security (MLS)]], [[Oblivious DNS over HTTPS]], [[Oblivious HTTP]], [[Privacy Preserving Measurement]], and TLS [[Encrypted Client Hello]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wood |first=Christopher |date=2022-02-24 |title=HPKE: Standardizing public-key encryption (finally!) |url=https://blog.cloudflare.com/hybrid-public-key-encryption/ |access-date=2025-09-21 |website=The Cloudflare Blog |language=en}}</ref>

Envelope encryption is an example of a usage of hybrid cryptosystems in [[cloud computing]]. In a cloud context, hybrid cryptosystems also enable centralized [[key management]].<ref name="Albertini">{{Cite journal|last1=Albertini|first1=Ange|last2=Duong|first2=Thai|last3=Gueron|first3=Shay|last4=Kölbl|first4=Stefan|last5=Luykx|first5=Atul|last6=Schmieg|first6=Sophie|date=November 17, 2020|title=How to Abuse and Fix Authenticated Encryption Without Key Commitment|url=https://eprint.iacr.org/2020/1456|journal=USENIX Security 2022|via=Cryptology ePrint Archive}}</ref><ref name=":222">{{Cite web|title=Envelope encryption {{!}} Cloud KMS Documentation|url=https://cloud.google.com/kms/docs/envelope-encryption|access-date=2021-12-30|website=Google Cloud|language=en}}</ref>

== Example ==
To encrypt a message addressed to Alice in a hybrid cryptosystem, Bob does the following:
# Obtains Alice's public key.
# Generates a fresh symmetric key for the data encapsulation scheme.
# Encrypts the message under the data encapsulation scheme, using the symmetric key just generated.
# Encrypts the symmetric key under the key encapsulation scheme, using Alice's public key.
# Sends both of these [[ciphertexts]] to Alice.

To decrypt this hybrid ciphertext, Alice does the following:
# Uses her private key to decrypt the symmetric key contained in the key encapsulation segment.
# Uses this symmetric key to decrypt the message contained in the data encapsulation segment.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=St Denis|first1=Tom|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/computer-science/hybrid-encryption|title=Cryptography for Developers|last2=Johnson|first2=Simon|publisher=Elsevier|year=2006|isbn=978-1-59749-104-4|chapter=9}}</ref><ref name=":0" />

==Security==

If both the key encapsulation and data encapsulation schemes in a hybrid cryptosystem are secure against [[adaptive chosen ciphertext attack]]s, then the hybrid scheme inherits that property as well.<ref name=cramer-shoup>{{cite journal
  | last = Cramer
  | first = Ronald
  |author2=Shoup, Victor
  | title = Design and Analysis of Practical Public-Key Encryption Schemes Secure against Adaptive Chosen Ciphertext Attack
  | journal = SIAM Journal on Computing
  | volume = 33
  | issue = 1
  | pages = 167–226
  | date = 2019
  | doi = 10.1137/S0097539702403773
  | url = http://www.shoup.net/papers/cca2.pdf | citeseerx = 10.1.1.76.8924
  }}</ref> However, it is possible to construct a hybrid scheme secure against adaptive chosen ciphertext attacks even if the key encapsulation has a slightly weakened security definition (though the security of the data encapsulation must be slightly stronger).<ref name=hofheinz-kiltz>{{cite conference
  | first = Dennis
  | last = Hofheinz
  |author2=Kiltz, Eike
  | title = Secure Hybrid Encryption from Weakened Key Encapsulation
  | book-title = Advances in Cryptology – CRYPTO 2007
  | pages = 553–571
  | publisher = Springer
  | date = 2019
  | url = https://www.iacr.org/archive/crypto2007/46220546/46220546.pdf
}}</ref>

== Envelope encryption ==
Envelope encryption is term used for encrypting with a hybrid cryptosystem used by all major [[cloud service provider]]s,<ref name="Albertini"/> often as part of a centralized [[key management]] system in cloud computing.<ref name=":13">{{Cite web|title=AWS KMS concepts - AWS Key Management Service|url=https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/concepts.html#enveloping|access-date=2021-12-30|website=docs.aws.amazon.com}}</ref>

Envelope encryption gives names to the keys used in hybrid encryption: Data Encryption Keys (abbreviated DEK, and used to encrypt data) and Key Encryption Keys (abbreviated KEK, and used to encrypt the DEKs). In a cloud environment, encryption with envelope encryption involves generating a DEK locally, encrypting one's data using the DEK, and then issuing a request to wrap (encrypt) the DEK with a KEK stored in a potentially more secure [[Service (computer science)|service]]. Then, this wrapped DEK and encrypted message constitute a [[ciphertext]] for the scheme. To decrypt a ciphertext, the wrapped DEK is unwrapped (decrypted) via a call to a service, and then the unwrapped DEK is used to decrypt the encrypted message.<ref name=":222"/> In addition to the normal advantages of a hybrid cryptosystem, using asymmetric encryption for the KEK in a cloud context provides easier key management and separation of roles, but can be slower.<ref name=":13"/>

In cloud systems, such as [[Google Cloud Platform]] and [[Amazon Web Services]], a key management system (KMS) can be available as a service.<ref name=":13"/><ref name=":222"/><ref>{{Cite web|title=What is envelope encryption? - FAQ{{!}} Alibaba Cloud Documentation Center|url=https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/doc-detail/42339.htm|access-date=2021-12-30|website=www.alibabacloud.com}}</ref> In some cases, the key management system will store keys in [[hardware security modules]], which are hardware systems that protect keys with hardware features like intrusion resistance.<ref>{{Cite web|last=|first=|title=Hardware Security Module (HSM) - Glossary {{!}} CSRC|url=https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/Hardware_Security_Module_HSM|access-date=2022-01-23|website=csrc.nist.gov|language=EN-US}}</ref> This means that KEKs can also be more secure because they are stored on secure specialized hardware.<ref name=":13" /> Envelope encryption makes centralized key management easier because a centralized key management system only needs to store KEKs, which occupy less space, and requests to the KMS only involve sending wrapped and unwrapped DEKs, which use less bandwidth than transmitting entire messages. Since one KEK can be used to encrypt many DEKs, this also allows for less storage space to be used in the KMS. This also allows for centralized auditing and [[access control]] at one point of access.<ref name=":222" />
